notes: One entry per (adapter, width, batch) the key-transform/state-update forward route was measured at, and only where the measured winner is not the structural default. `route` is the winning graph, from the three candidates the stage builds: `wide-fused` is the wider-group fused kernel (64 / head_size heads per workgroup, all 64 lanes in both phases), `narrow-fused` is the one-workgroup-per-head kernel it replaced, and `staged` is the two-dispatch chain (`key_transform_forward` then `state_forward`). `candidates` holds each candidate's measured median milliseconds, so the recorded route has to agree with the measurement that produced it; the loader rejects an entry whose route is not its fastest candidate. Naming each fused arm as its own route is what replaced the earlier compose-plus-arm pair. On this Intel Gen9 part the wider group now wins at every batch up to 16 -- its all-lane transform phase removed both the batch-16 crossover and the reason the narrow arm existed -- while batch 32, where the launch is throughput-bound, still favours the chain; the staged entry is why the shipped default dispatches two kernels there. An entry may carry `parameter_storage` to scope the whole route, arm included, to one storage policy; the policy-less entry is what every other policy reads. An empty list means no adapter has been measured yet, and a device with no entry keeps the structural default: the fusion with the wider-group arm. A geometry measured inside the 2% noise band is a tie and carries no entry at all. Re-record a new adapter's own entries with `--record-decisions`. Phase-level GPU time behind these numbers is in `key_state_forward_profile.json` (`validation/profile_rwkv_key_state_forward.py`).
